name: Adaptive and Maladaptive Emotions, Behaviours and Cognitions
what: This subtopic examines what it means to be adaptive or maladaptive across three domains of psychological development: emotions, behaviours, and cognitions. It also explores how adaptiveness is always assessed relative to age, developmental stage, and situational context.
why: Adaptive functioning is closely linked to normality, but whether something is adaptive or maladaptive is not fixed. The same action can be adaptive in one context and maladaptive in another, and understanding this prevents oversimplified judgements about psychological development.

items.title: I can define adaptive and maladaptive and apply these terms to psychological development
items.what: Adaptive means being able to adjust to the environment appropriately and function effectively. Maladaptive means being unable to adapt to the environment appropriately and function effectively. Both terms relate to how well an individual can meet the changing demands of their life.
items.why: These terms provide a functional lens for assessing whether a person's psychological responses are helping or hindering them. They complement the typical/atypical distinction by focusing on consequences rather than just deviation from norms.
items.example: A child on their first day of school who gets their own lunchbox and eats independently is showing adaptive behaviour. A child who refuses to eat unless a teacher feeds them is showing maladaptive behaviour, because it prevents them from functioning independently in their new environment.

items.title: I can give examples of adaptive and maladaptive emotions
items.what: Adaptive emotions are those that are effectively regulated and displayed in a way that helps the individual cope with their circumstances. Maladaptive emotions are those that are poorly regulated or disproportionate in intensity or duration, hindering the individual's functioning.
items.why: Emotions such as sadness, worry, and fear are adaptive in many situations because they help people confront and manage threats. However, when these emotions persist for prolonged periods and begin to interfere with daily life, they become maladaptive and may indicate a mental health condition.
items.example: Feeling angry after being refused a new phone and calming down within a few hours using coping strategies is an adaptive emotional response. Staying intensely angry at a parent for a full month over the same event, to the point of refusing to speak to them or attend school, would be maladaptive.

items.title: I can give examples of adaptive and maladaptive behaviours
items.what: Adaptive behaviours are activities that enhance an individual's ability to meet the changing demands of their everyday life. Maladaptive behaviours are activities that hinder this ability and prevent effective functioning.
items.why: Identifying whether a behaviour is adaptive or maladaptive helps determine whether intervention is warranted. A behaviour that appears concerning on the surface may actually be adaptive, and an apparently harmless behaviour may be quietly undermining a person's functioning.
items.example: Going for a social drink after work to unwind and connect with colleagues is an adaptive behaviour. Drinking to the point of being unable to function at work the following day is maladaptive, because it prevents the person from meeting their professional obligations.

items.title: I can give examples of adaptive and maladaptive cognitions
items.what: Adaptive cognitions involve having awareness and knowledge that helps the individual adjust to different environments and situations. Maladaptive cognitions involve unhelpful thought patterns that make adjustment more difficult and distort interpretation of events.
items.why: Thought patterns directly influence emotional responses and behaviour. Maladaptive cognitions, such as catastrophising or overgeneralising, can drive a cycle of dysfunction even when external circumstances are manageable.
items.example: After failing a maths test, thinking 'this is feedback that I need to study differently' is an adaptive cognition that supports future improvement. Thinking 'I failed this test so I will never get a job' is a maladaptive cognition that is disproportionate to the evidence and likely to increase distress and reduce motivation.

items.title: I can explain why whether something is adaptive or maladaptive depends on age, context, and developmental stage
items.what: Adaptiveness is not fixed. The same behaviour can be adaptive at one age and maladaptive at another, and adaptive in one situation but maladaptive in another. Assessment must always consider the developmental stage and situational context of the individual.
items.why: Applying a single standard of adaptive behaviour across all ages and contexts produces inaccurate assessments. What is functional and expected for a toddler is not the same as what is functional and expected for a teenager or adult.
items.example: Crying and throwing a tantrum when lost in a supermarket is adaptive for a three-year-old, because crying is an effective way to attract an adult's attention in that situation. The same behaviour in a seventeen-year-old is maladaptive, because they have access to more effective strategies such as approaching a staff member or using a phone to call a guardian.

items.title: I can explain why some apparently maladaptive behaviours may actually be adaptive for specific individuals
items.what: A behaviour that appears maladaptive in a general context may be adaptive for a particular individual based on their neurological profile, developmental history, or situational needs. Assessment must consider the function a behaviour serves for that specific person.
items.why: Applying a universal standard of adaptiveness without considering individual differences can lead to misclassification. A behaviour that disrupts others or appears non-functional may be serving an important regulatory or coping function for the individual.
items.example: A student rocking back and forth in a quiet classroom might appear maladaptive because it is disruptive and suggests they are not adjusting to the environment. However, for a student with autism, this behaviour (known as stimming) may be adaptive, as it helps them emotionally regulate and return to a functional state in an overstimulating environment.
